message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick‑Reference Overview**

| Category | Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u | Weighted average of the three naturally occurring isotopes. |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ | One valence electron. |
| | Ionization energy (1st) | 13.598 eV | Highest among all elements. |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV | Smallest of all elements. |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 | Highest of all elements. |
| | Atomic radius | ~31 pm (covalent) | Very small due to single electron. |
| | Van der Waals radius | ~120 pm | For H₂ molecules. |
| **Physical Properties (at 25 °C, 1 atm)** | State | Gas | Colorless, odorless, tasteless. |
| | Density | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ | Lowest of all gases. |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C | Extremely low; requires cryogenic temperatures. |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C | Extremely low; solidifies only at very low temperatures. |
| | Specific heat (gas) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | High compared to other gases. |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.425 kJ mol⁻¹ | Very low. |
| | Speed of sound | ~1270 m s⁻¹ | Fastest among gases. |
| | Solubility in water | 1.6 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0015 M) | Very low; slightly soluble. |
| | Refractive index | 1.000132 | Slightly above vacuum. |
| | Magnetic susceptibility | Diamagnetic | Weakly repelled by magnetic fields. |
| **Chemical Properties** | Bond type | Diatomic (H₂) | Covalent, single bond. |
| | Bond dissociation energy | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Strong but not as strong as O₂. |
| | Oxidation states | +1, –1 | Forms hydrides (–1) and acids (–1). |
| | Acidic behavior | Forms H⁺ (proton) | Strong acid when dissolved in water (hydronium). |
| | Basic behavior | Forms H⁻ (hydride) | Strong base when combined with metals. |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive with nonmetals (O₂, N₂, Cl₂) | Forms oxides, nitrides, halides. |
| | Combustion | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O | Exothermic, releases ~286 kJ mol⁻¹. |
| | Hydrogen bonding | Forms weak H–H bonds in H₂O, NH₃, HF | Key to many physical properties. |
| | Isotopic chemistry | Deuterium (D) and Tritium (T) behave similarly but differ in mass. | Deuterium used in NMR, tritium in nuclear fusion. |
| **Isotopes** | **¹H (Protium)** | Stable | Most abundant (~99.98 %). |
| | **²H (Deuterium)** | Stable | ~0.015 % natural abundance. |
| | **³H (Tritium)** | Radioactive (half‑life 12.32 y) | Used in nuclear fusion, radiolabeling. |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Nuclear spin | ½ (¹H), 1 (²H), ½ (³H) | Determines NMR behavior. |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.7928 µ_N (¹H) | Large for a single proton. |
| | Binding energy per nucleon | ~7.98 MeV | Low compared to heavier nuclei. |
| **Applications & Significance** | Energy carrier | Hydrogen fuel cells, rocket propellant | Clean energy potential. |
| | Industrial uses | Production of ammonia (Haber process), methanol, hydrogenation reactions | Key in chemical industry. |
| | Scientific research | Standard for NMR, quantum chemistry, astrophysics (interstellar H₂) | Fundamental element in physics. |
| | Astrophysics | Most abundant element in the universe | Dominates stellar interiors. |
| | Environmental impact | Combustion produces only water vapor | Potentially zero‑emission fuel. |

---

### Quick Takeaways

1. **Atomic Simplicity** – Hydrogen has only one proton and one electron, making it the simplest atom and a benchmark for quantum mechanical calculations.
2. **Extreme Physical Properties** – Its low boiling/melting points and high speed of sound reflect its lightness and weak intermolecular forces.
3. **Chemical Versatility** – Despite being a single‑electron system, hydrogen forms a wide range of compounds: acids (H⁺), bases (H⁻), covalent molecules (H₂), and ionic salts (NaH, CaH₂).
4. **Isotopic Diversity** – Deuterium and tritium introduce mass-dependent chemistry and nuclear physics phenomena.
5. **Energy Potential** – Hydrogen’s combustion yields only water, positioning it as a clean energy vector, though storage and infrastructure remain challenges.

Feel free to ask for deeper dives into any specific property (e.g., spectroscopic constants, thermodynamic data, or industrial processes)!
